vignette:
Imran had spent most of his adult life working in non-profit settings, the kind of work that kept him in community centers, offices, and other people's homes, but the attack that now shaped his days had happened in a place that had once felt ordinary and safe. In his late sixties, after a divorce that left him living alone, he was raped by a man who had gained access to him unexpectedly, and what stayed with Imran was not only the assault itself but the helplessness of being trapped, touched, and unable to make sense of what was happening quickly enough to stop it. Since then, he had come to believe that his reactions proved he was a lousy coper, that something in him had broken beyond repair, and that he was permanently an outsider now. He told himself he would never be able to feel normal emotions again, only a narrow band of panic, numbness, and shame, and those beliefs spread into almost everything he did. They made him avoid being alone in a room or building, because solitude felt like the condition in which danger could happen again; they also pushed him to always sit with his back against a wall so he could see the room, as if vigilance might substitute for safety. When the feelings became overwhelming, he hurt himself physically to release them, later ashamed that even this relief seemed to confirm how badly he was managing.

The memories arrived in fragments he could not fully shape into words. Imran knew what happened, but when he tried to describe it, he would stall, as though language could not reach the core of it. Sometimes, while he was trying to speak, he would hear the sounds from the assault in his mind, as if the frightening event were replaying itself acoustically, and with that came a dull physical pain in the same parts of his body that had been injured then. Those sensory returns deepened his conviction that he was damaged, and they also made him more alert to anything that sounded like another person entering his home. He began listening for footsteps, the creak of a door, the rustle that meant someone might be coming in, especially at night, and he was on high alert when unexpected or loud sounds cut through the quiet. A dropped object in the hallway, a shouted voice outside his apartment, even the sudden slam of a car door could make him freeze and scan the space. Because he was already expecting danger, he heard more threats than most people would, and each sharp sound seemed to confirm what he feared: that he was no longer safe in the world and had no reliable way of protecting himself.

The more Imran monitored the environment, the more tightly his life narrowed. He arranged his chair in meetings, at home, and in the office so that his back was against a wall, a habit that gave him the illusion of seeing trouble before it reached him. He avoided staying alone after work and found excuses not to be the last person in the building, because empty rooms and quiet corridors made him feel exposed. Yet those same efforts kept the event alive in his mind. When he was alone and listening hard, any small sound could pull him back into the memory, and once the memory had started, the familiar sounds, the bodily pain, and the sense of being trapped all rushed in together. Afterward he would think again that he was a bad coper, which made him withdraw further, and the withdrawal only left him with more time to listen for signs of entry, more time to notice every unexpected noise, more time to feel the memory hovering just under the surface. Even at his non-profit job, where he used to move easily between meetings and community visits, he now chose seating and routes around the building with unusual care, scanning doorways and guarding himself against being touched unexpectedly by colleagues who might tap his shoulder in passing. That startle response made him seem tense and distant, which he interpreted as further proof that he was an outsider and would never feel normal again.

By the time he sought help, Imran's world had become organized around avoiding the next surge of terror, and he was exhausted by the effort. He came in because the nightmares, the self-injury, and the constant watching had started to affect his work and his ability to be around people without feeling cornered. What he feared most was that his mind and body had learned to live as if the rape were still happening, and what he hoped for, reluctantly but urgently, was some way to hear a sound, feel a touch, or sit alone in a room without immediately believing danger was at the door.
